messages.content: Write the opening pitch section of a README for a new open source charting library. Around 200 words.

# Kestrel

Kestrel draws charts. It doesn't manage your state, claim your DOM, or ship a theme system you'll spend a week fighting.

Hand it an array of objects and two accessor functions; it hands back SVG. Marks — bars, lines, areas, ribbons, whatever you write yourself — are plain functions of scale and data. A candlestick chart with an annotation layer and a broken axis is four calls, not a hunt through a 400-key config object for the flag that turns it on.

The runtime is 9 kB gzipped, with no dependencies beyond a vendored fork of d3-scale. Output is a string on both sides of the wire, so a chart renders identically in Node and in the browser. Point it at a build script and you get an SVG file ready to rasterize. Point it at React and you get elements.

It exists because we had a dashboard with 60 small multiples, and every established library either blew the frame budget or made us rewrite the same 200 lines of margin arithmetic sixty times.

Need a chart in one line? Chart.js is right there. Need to say exactly what the picture is? Keep reading.

---

Two things to replace before release: the name and the numbers. The 9 kB, the d3-scale fork, and the 60-small-multiples anecdote are placeholders. Swap in your real ones rather than deleting them; the specifics are what keep this off the pile of interchangeable library homepages.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
# Kestrel

Kestrel draws charts. That's the whole job. It won't hold your state, take over a div, or hand you a theme system to argue with for a week.

Give it an array of objects and two accessor functions; you get SVG back. Marks — bars, lines, areas, ribbons, anything you write yourself — are functions of a scale and some data. Want a candlestick chart with an annotation layer and a broken axis? Four calls. Not an afternoon spent grepping a 400-key config object for whichever flag switches it on.

9 kB gzipped at runtime, and the only dependency is a vendored fork of d3-scale. Output is a string on both ends of the wire, so a chart comes out identical in Node and in the browser. Run it from a build script, get an SVG file ready to rasterize. Run it under React, get elements.

Why it exists: we had a dashboard with 60 small multiples, and every mature library we tried either ate the frame budget or made us write the same 200 lines of margin arithmetic sixty times over.

Want a chart in one line? Go use Chart.js. Want to say exactly what the picture is? Read on.

---

Two things to swap before release: the name and the numbers. The 9 kB, the d3-scale fork, and the 60-small-multiples story are stand-ins. Replace them with your own — don't just cut them. Those specifics are the only reason this page won't read like every other library homepage.
